label: GPT-6.1 Sol
output:
# Bistro kitchens run on bar fridges and spite

Jonno,

You can stop messaging me about the coolroom now. Here’s the whole thing, written down so I never have to type it again. Get yourself a pint that costs nineteen Australian dollars and settle in.

And before you start with “I would’ve sorted that”, you wouldn’t have. London has made you soft. You’ve been gone since February and I reckon you’d need a little sit-down if someone asked you to change a gas bottle now.

The coolroom compressor died overnight Monday into Tuesday. Cup Day. Naturally. Couldn’t have done it on a quiet Wednesday when we had twenty-six booked and half of them were going to order chips. Had to pick the day we had 140 covers coming in for a three-course set lunch.

I found it at 6.40 in the morning.

Eleven degrees.

You know that moment where you look at a thermometer and briefly decide you don’t know how numbers work? I stood there giving it another chance. Like maybe eleven was going to turn into three if I wasn’t a dick about it.

It stayed eleven.

Raff was away, so I was running the kitchen. This was a fun little addition to the day’s responsibilities. Normally you start by checking the prep list. I got to start by ringing a fridge bloke and trying to work out how much of lunch was going in the bin.

Wally from Coldline couldn’t come until Wednesday. Part had to come from Sydney.

Nothing against Wally. He was straight with me. But “part coming from Sydney” is a fairly grim collection of words when there are 140 people due in and your coolroom has decided it’s a cupboard.

Phil’s contribution was, “Just make it work, mate.”

Cheers, Phil. Hadn’t thought of that. I was going to put a little hat on the compressor and see if it fancied having another go, but your thing sounds better.

“Just make it work” is not a plan. It’s what someone says before walking away from the bit where a plan is needed.

Anyway, we started shifting everything we could keep. Checked it, sorted it, found somewhere cold for it. Both undercounters were packed. The bar fridge got promoted well beyond its qualifications. Marta next door let us use half her walk-in, which is the main reason this is a blog post about a good service rather than me advertising kitchen equipment on Marketplace.

We still lost about eighteen hundred bucks’ worth of stock. Mostly dairy and the duck legs. That bit wasn’t funny. There’s no entertaining way to chuck that much food, so we did it, swore about it and kept moving.

The beef shin, meanwhile, needed a change of address.

Thirty kilos of it. Me and Benny. Down the laneway. In the rain. On a milk crate trolley.

You remember the trolley. You’d have looked at it and said it was fucked, then used it anyway. So don’t get superior.

We were halfway through this very professional food transport operation when one wheel fell off.

Not got a bit wobbly. Fell off. Finished its employment with us right there.

Benny and I were left holding thirty kilos of beef on a trolley that now had strong opinions about which direction it wanted to go. Rain coming down, wheel off doing its own thing, both of us trying not to tip lunch into the lane.

I did think of you then. Mainly because you’d have been absolutely useless from laughing. You always liked a disaster best when someone else was physically underneath it.

We got the beef where it needed to go. I’m telling you that now because apparently watching two chefs wrestle it past a window raises questions about provenance.

More on that shortly.

Kev went to the servo for ice and came back with fourteen bags for the old esky. Fourteen. The bloke at the servo asked if we were having a party.

I wish he’d come along. Could’ve helped carry something.

Kev just got on with it. No performance, no wandering around saying how fucked we were, just ice into the esky and back to work. Everyone had something to do and, for once, nobody needed to be told the same thing six times.

You would have hated how inspiring it was. Very bad environment for your whole “this place is run by idiots” routine. Although you could still have pointed at Phil.

By the time lunch came around, we had food spread across two undercounters, the bar fridge and Marta’s walk-in. Getting anything required knowing where it had ended up and whether someone was already going next door. We were running a bistro and a small, angry courier service.

Then at 12.15 we had to 86 the panna cotta.

On a set menu.

For 140.

Lovely.

Dessert became “affogato with whatever”, which is not how it was described to customers but is the name I’ll be using forever.

And they loved it.

Of course they did.

All that effort that goes into planning a dessert, getting it right, making it look decent, and apparently what people really want is coffee, ice cream and whatever else we can put near it while under pressure.

I’m not saying we should stop trying. I am saying the panna cotta took this whole thing worse than anyone.

Table nine provided the other highlight. A lady who’d seen us out the window asked if the beef was “free range from the laneway”.

Fair play to her. Can’t complain about customers not understanding where their food comes from and then get precious when one witnesses the delivery process.

I’d like you to know she got a better line out of it than you’ve managed in the several messages you’ve sent me. “Cool story bro” doesn’t count as material. Neither does sending the ice cube emoji eight times.

The really annoying part is that it was probably the best service we did all year.

Genuinely.

Not “good considering”. Good. Everyone was locked in. Benny was all over it. Kev kept things moving. People called what they needed, listened to the answer and did their jobs. There wasn’t room for anyone to have their usual little detour into being a pain in the arse.

We had every reason for it to go sideways, and it didn’t.

I’m proud of that. Don’t make it weird.

You know what a kitchen’s like when it’s actually working properly. Not quiet, obviously. Still hot, still loud, still someone needing to get past you at the exact wrong time. But you’re not dragging each other through it. You look up and the thing you were about to ask for is already happening.

We had that.

You’d have enjoyed it once you’d finished crying about the coolroom. Probably would’ve done your little lap after service pretending you hadn’t been worried.

Marta is getting paid back in croissant credit. I don’t fully understand the exchange rate, but I owe her about three weeks of staff meal. She’s earned it. Half a walk-in on Cup Day buys you a fair bit of goodwill, and apparently ongoing access to our labour.

Then there was the sweep.

My horse was called Ice Cold Lad.

Obviously it was.

After spending the whole day trying to keep things cold, I had actual money riding on something called Ice Cold Lad. Came second last. Couldn’t even commit to being the worst.

I don’t follow racing closely enough to know whether a horse can take the piss, but that one managed it.

So that’s what happened. We lost stock, borrowed refrigeration off everyone except the florist, pushed beef through the rain on three wheels and accidentally improved dessert. Fed 140 people. Had a cracking service. I acquired a substantial croissant debt.

Bistro kitchens run on bar fridges and spite. I’ve got evidence now.

Anyway, hope London’s good. Hope you’re enjoying telling people you’re from Melbourne before they’ve asked, and whatever else you do over there instead of being useful here.

You missed a good one.

Come home, ya flog.
